{{Short description|Products of numbers of the form a^2 + nb^2 are also of that form}}

In [[algebra]], '''Brahmagupta's identity''' says that, for given {{mvar|n}}, the product of two numbers of the form {{math|''a''{{sup|2}} + ''nb''{{sup|2}}}} is itself a number of that form. In other words, the set of such numbers is [[closure (mathematics)|closed]] under multiplication. Specifically:

<math display=block>(a^2 + nb^2)(c^2 + nd^2) = (ac \pm nbd)^2 + n(ad \mp bc)^2.</math>

This identity holds in both the [[integer|ring of integers]] and the [[rational number|ring of rational numbers]], and more generally in any [[commutative ring]].

Also, it can be viewed as a special case of the following identity:

<math display=block>(ha^2 + kb^2)(hc^2 + kd^2) = (hac \pm kbd)^2 + hk(ad \mp bc)^2.</math>

==History==
The identity is a generalization of the so-called [[Brahmagupta–Fibonacci identity|Brahmagupta-Fibonacci identity]] (where {{math|1=''n'' = 1}}) which is actually found in [[Diophantus]]' ''[[Arithmetica]]'' (III, 19).
That identity was rediscovered by [[Brahmagupta]] (598&ndash;668), an [[Indian mathematicians|Indian mathematician]] and [[Indian astronomy|astronomer]], who generalized it and used it in his study of what is now called [[Pell's equation]]. His ''[[Brahmasphutasiddhanta]]'' was translated from [[Sanskrit]] into [[Arabic language|Arabic]] by [[Mohammad al-Fazari]], and was subsequently translated into [[Latin]] in 1126.<ref>{{cite book |last=Joseph |first=George Gheverghese |author-link=George Gheverghese Joseph |title=The Crest of the Peacock |title-link=The Crest of the Peacock |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |year=2000 |isbn=0-691-00659-8 |page=306}}</ref> The identity later appeared in [[Fibonacci]]'s ''[[The Book of Squares|Book of Squares]]'' in 1225.

== Application to Pell's equation ==
In its original context, Brahmagupta applied his discovery to the solution of what was later called [[Pell's equation]], namely {{math|1=''x''<sup>2</sup> &minus; ''Ny''<sup>2</sup> = 1}}. Using the identity in the form

<math display=block>(x_1^2 - Ny_1^2)(x_2^2 - Ny_2^2) = (x_1x_2 + Ny_1y_2)^2 - N(x_1y_2 + x_2y_1)^2, </math>

he was able to "compose" triples {{math|(''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''y''<sub>1</sub>, ''k''<sub>1</sub>)}} and {{math|(''x''<sub>2</sub>, ''y''<sub>2</sub>, ''k''<sub>2</sub>)}} that were solutions of {{math|1=''x''<sup>2</sup> &minus; ''Ny''<sup>2</sup> = ''k''}}, to generate the new triple

<math display=block>(x_1x_2 + Ny_1y_2,\, x_1y_2 + x_2y_1,\, k_1k_2).</math>

Not only did this give a way to generate infinitely many solutions to {{math|1=''x''<sup>2</sup> &minus; ''Ny''<sup>2</sup> = 1}} starting with one solution, but also, by dividing such a composition by {{math|''k''<sub>1</sub>''k''<sub>2</sub>}}, integer or "nearly integer" solutions could often be obtained. The general method for solving the Pell equation given by [[Bhaskara II]] in 1150, namely the [[chakravala method|chakravala (cyclic) method]], was also based on this identity.<ref name=stillwell>{{citation | year=2002 | title = Mathematics and its history | author1=[[John Stillwell]] | edition=2 | publisher=Springer | isbn=978-0-387-95336-6 | pages=72–76 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WNjRrqTm62QC&pg=PA72}}</ref>
